text.text: The office of a home inspection company: every booking with its agreement and payment, reports delivered on time, the agents who refer you, and the licenses, insurance and tool calibrations that keep you allowed to work.

This workspace runs the business side of a home inspection company: who is booked where, whether the agreement is signed and the fee paid, which reports are still being written, which agents send you work, and when each license, policy and tool calibration renews. Your report software still writes the reports.

text.text: Three rules the office never breaks
No inspection happens without a signed agreement.
No report is released before the fee is paid, unless the agreement says it is paid at closing.
Reports go out within 24 hours of the inspection.
Enter every booked inspection with address, size, year built and add-ons.
Add your referral partners with the date you last spoke.
Add every license, insurance policy and calibration date. One missed renewal can stop the business.

Most problems on inspection day start at booking: wrong address, utilities off, no access, or a client who never signed the agreement. A complete booking prevents them.

Type: full home, pre-listing, condo or re-inspection
Add-on services: radon, sewer scope, termite, mold sampling, pool and spa
The contract's inspection deadline, so you know how much room there is
Price by size and age, then add each add-on. Older homes on crawlspaces take longer; price for the time. Quote the total before booking so there is no surprise on the invoice.

text.text: A re-inspection checks only the repairs the seller agreed to make. Book it with the repair list attached and price it as a short visit.

The Cypress Hollow pre-listing is booked for this week with a sewer scope, but the agreement is still unsigned. The scheduler resends it and calls the seller, because the inspector will not start without it.
Note why every cancelled job fell through: deal fell apart, price, or another inspector. Patterns tell you whether to change your prices or your follow-up.
The report is your product. Agents judge you on how fast it arrives and how clearly it reads; buyers judge you on whether it is fair.
Every report is delivered within 24 hours of the inspection, and the same evening when the contract deadline is tight.
Photograph every defect with something for scale, plus the data plates on the furnace, water heater and electrical panel.
Record the age and condition of the roof, heating and cooling, water heater and electrical panel.
Count safety items as you go: missing smoke alarms, double-tapped breakers, missing handrails, gas leaks.
Lead with a summary of major defects and safety items. Enter the count in
Describe each defect in plain words: what it is, where it is, why it matters and who should look at it.
Avoid alarming language. "Recommend evaluation by a licensed electrician" is more useful than "dangerous".
Stay within your standards of practice. Do not estimate repair costs unless that is your service.
Fee paid, or the agreement says paid at closing
Spelling of names and the address checked
The summary agrees with the body
and send it to the client and, with the client's permission, their agent.
Offer a short call to walk the buyer through the summary. Most buyers have never read a report before, and ten minutes on the phone is what they remember.

Corbel Street was inspected two days ago and is still in Writing report with four safety items. The fee is unpaid, so the office calls the buyer first and the report goes out the moment payment clears.
Once a month, count reports delivered late. Anything above one in twenty means the schedule is too full.
Most inspection companies get most of their work from a small group of agents. Treat them like your best customers, because they are.
Any agent who has sent you a client. Add them with brokerage, phone and email, and pick a
date. The overdue view lists everyone you have let slip.
Each week, contact at least two partners: a call, a coffee, or a visit to their office meeting.
and pick the next date: two weeks for top referrers, a month for regulars, six weeks for new partners.
A sample report so they can show buyers what to expect.
A short talk at their team meeting: the five defects that most often stall a sale and how to prepare sellers for them.
A fast answer when their buyer has a question about your report.

Agents refer clients; buyers hire you. Your report is written for the buyer, never softened for the agent. Agents who want softer reports are not partners worth keeping. Never pay or give anything of value for referrals where your state forbids it.

text.text: Tobias at Copperline Homes was due a call two days ago and has two jobs coming up. The owner calls to thank him and offers a short talk at his office's sales meeting.
When a regular partner goes quiet for two months, ask directly whether something went wrong. A late report or a buyer who felt scared is usually the reason, and it is often fixable.
An expired license means you may not inspect. Lapsed insurance means one claim can end the company. Uncalibrated tools mean findings you cannot defend. This page keeps all three current.

License: that inspector stops inspecting until it is renewed. Reassign their bookings.
Insurance: call the broker the same day.
Calibration: use a backup tool or remove that service from bookings until it is back.
and set the new date once it is renewed.
The moisture meter's calibration was due six days ago. Rani sends it to the lab and uses the spare meter in the meantime. The thermal camera is due this week, so it goes out together with the meter.

Add up the yearly cost of every license, policy, calibration and subscription on this page and divide it by the number of inspections you expect. That small amount belongs in every inspection price, so renewals are never a surprise.
Store a scan of every license, policy and calibration certificate where the whole office can reach it. Agents and clients sometimes ask, and an answer within minutes looks professional.
